parts.label: A
parts.prompt: A researcher plans a study of students at a large high school. For each person the researcher records whether a student exercises before school and the number of hours of sleep the previous night. Identify the explanatory variable and the response variable in this study.
parts.model_answer: Explanatory variable: whether a student exercises before school. Response variable: the number of hours of sleep the previous night.

rubric_rows.criterion: Identifies the explanatory variable as whether a student exercises before school
required_elements: whether a student exercises before school

rubric_rows.criterion: Identifies the response variable as the number of hours of sleep the previous night
required_elements: number of hours of sleep the previous night
common_errors: names the group as the response

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: The table shown gives the five-number summary of the number of hours of sleep the previous night for the sample of students at a large high school in the study. (i) Calculate the interquartile range. (ii) Is a value of $105$ hours an outlier according to the $1.5\times\mathrm{IQR}$ rule? Justify your answer with a calculation.
parts.model_answer: (i) IQR = 87 - 73 = 14. (ii) The upper boundary is 87 + 1.5(14) = 108; since 105 is not greater than 108, 105 is not an outlier.

rubric_rows.criterion: Calculates the interquartile range (answer 14)
common_errors: uses the range instead of the IQR

rubric_rows.criterion: Compares 105 with the boundary Q3 + 1.5 IQR = 108 and states that it is not an outlier

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: The researcher is considering an experiment with $80$ volunteers from all students at the school. (i) Describe a method to assign each volunteer at random to one of the two groups so that the groups are the same size. (ii) Explain why random assignment makes it reasonable to conclude that a difference in the number of hours of sleep the previous night was caused by the treatment.
parts.model_answer: (i) Number the volunteers, use a random number generator (or draw names from a hat) to choose half of them for the treatment group; the rest form the other group. (ii) Random assignment tends to balance other variables across the groups, so a difference in the response is attributable to the treatment.

rubric_rows.criterion: Describes a chance method (random numbers, names from a hat) that puts half of the volunteers in each group
alt_solutions: shuffle names and take the first half

rubric_rows.criterion: Explains that random assignment balances other (lurking) variables between the groups so cause and effect can be concluded
common_errors: says random assignment makes the sample representative of the population

parts.label: D
parts.prompt: Suppose that instead the researcher simply compares the students at a large high school in the study who already exercise before school with those who do not exercise before school. Can the researcher conclude that whether a student exercises before school causes a change in the number of hours of sleep the previous night? Justify your answer.
parts.model_answer: No. This is an observational study; the groups chose themselves, so other variables (confounders) may explain the difference and a cause-and-effect conclusion is not justified.

rubric_rows.criterion: States that a cause-and-effect conclusion is not justified because the individuals chose their own groups (observational study, confounding possible)

common_errors: names only the sample or one individual

payload.title: Linear regression of exam score on number of hours of study

stimulus.description: Scatterplot of exam score (points) versus number of hours of study for 18 observations, with the least-squares regression line.

data.title: Exam score versus hours of study

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: The least-squares regression line for the data in the scatterplot shown is $\hat y = 46.47 + 4.81x$, where $x$ is the number of hours of study and $\hat y$ is the predicted exam score (points), and $r^2 = 0.47$. Interpret the slope of the line in the context of the data.
parts.model_answer: For each additional hour, the predicted exam score increases by about 4.81 points.

rubric_rows.criterion: States that the predicted response changes by 4.81 for each one-unit increase in the explanatory variable (with the correct direction)
Gives the interpretation in context with units (predicted value, points, per hour)
common_errors: omits the word predicted or the context

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: (i) Use the regression line to predict the exam score when $x = 5$. (ii) One observation has $x = 5$ and an actual exam score of $52.8$. Calculate the residual for this observation.
parts.model_answer: (i) Predicted value: 46.47 + (4.81)(5) = 70.52. (ii) Residual = actual - predicted = 52.8 - 70.52 = -17.72.

rubric_rows.criterion: Calculates the predicted value (answer 70.52)
common_errors: uses the slope as the intercept

rubric_rows.criterion: Calculates the residual as actual minus predicted (answer -17.72)

payload.title: Survey of students: probability and a confidence interval

stimulus.description: Two-way table of group and response for 278 students.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: The two-way display shown summarizes a survey of $278$ students. One student is selected at random. Given that the selected student is a freshman, what is the probability that the student plays a sport? Round to three decimal places.

rubric_rows.criterion: Restricts to the group total (181) as the denominator
Calculates the conditional probability (answer 0.420)

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Overall, the proportion of the $278$ students who play a sport is $0.453$. Are the events 'the student is a freshman' and 'the student plays a sport' independent? Justify your answer using probabilities from the display.
parts.model_answer: No. The conditional probability $0.420$ is not equal to the overall probability $0.453$, so the events are not independent.

rubric_rows.criterion: Compares the conditional probability (0.420) with the overall probability (0.453)
Concludes the events are not independent because the two probabilities are not equal
common_errors: says events are not independent because they can occur together

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: Suppose $6$ students are selected at random with replacement. Let $X$ be the number of them who play a sport, and use $p = 0.45$. Identify the distribution of $X$ and calculate the probability that at least $2$ of the $6$ students play a sport.
parts.model_answer: $X$ is binomial with $n=6$ and $p=0.45$. $P(X \ge 2) = 1 - P(0) - P(1) \approx 0.836$.

rubric_rows.criterion: Identifies a binomial distribution with n = 6 and p = 0.45
common_errors: gives p as the conditional probability

rubric_rows.criterion: Calculates the probability of at least 2 (answer 0.836)

parts.label: D
parts.prompt: Treat the survey data for the freshmen as a random sample from all freshmen. Calculate a $95\%$ confidence interval for the proportion of all freshmen who play a sport. Round the endpoints to three decimal places.

rubric_rows.criterion: Identifies a one-sample z-interval for a proportion with the sample proportion in the center and the standard error with the sample proportion
common_errors: uses p0 in the standard error

rubric_rows.criterion: Calculates the interval (answer (0.348, 0.492))

parts.label: E
parts.prompt: Interpret the interval from part (D) in the context of the survey, including the meaning of the confidence level.
parts.model_answer: We are $95\%$ confident that the interval from 0.348 to 0.492 captures the true proportion of all freshmen who play a sport. The method captures the true proportion in about $95\%$ of all random samples.

rubric_rows.criterion: Interprets the interval as capturing the population proportion for the group in context
common_errors: interprets the interval as a range for the sample proportion

rubric_rows.criterion: Explains the confidence level as the long-run success rate of the method (about 95% of random samples)
required_elements: 95% of intervals from random samples capture the parameter
